config.title: Observability — Logs, Metrics & Traces

intro.title: Observability — Logs, Metrics & Traces
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a simple observability dashboard to monitor a simulated web service. You will learn the core concepts of observability: logs for recording events, metrics for measuring performance, and traces for tracking requests. The main technologies involved are structured logging, basic metric collection, and distributed tracing. By the end, you will understand how these three pillars work together to provide visibility into system health and behavior. This foundational knowledge is essential for debugging and maintaining reliable production systems.
intro.usecase: In production systems, observability tools are critical for monitoring application health and troubleshooting issues. Developers use log aggregation dashboards like Splunk or Datadog to search through application logs when debugging errors. Metrics dashboards with charts and graphs in tools like Grafana or Prometheus visualize system performance trends over time. Distributed tracing interfaces in tools like Jaeger or Zipkin help engineers follow request flows across microservices to identify bottlenecks. These observability interfaces are essential for maintaining reliable, high-performance applications in production environments.

objectives: Implement structured logging in a sample application
Configure metrics collection for key performance indicators
Construct distributed traces to track request flows
Integrate logging, metrics, and tracing into a unified observability dashboard
Manipulate log levels to control verbosity in different environments
Initialize alerting rules based on metric thresholds
Render trace visualizations to identify latency bottlenecks

steps.title: Import React and useState
steps.instruction: Import React and useState from 'react' to prepare for state management in our observability dashboard.
steps.hint: Use the import statement to bring in both React and the useState hook from the 'react' package.
steps.analogousExample:
// Importing React and hooks
import React, { useState } from 'react';
steps.expectedOutcome: The React library and useState hook are imported and ready to use.
successCriteria: React and useState are imported from 'react'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully imported React and useState, which are essential for building interactive observability components.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure you're importing both React and useState from the 'react' package.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's try again. You need to import both React and useState from 'react' to proceed.

steps.title: Create main ObservabilityDashboard component
steps.instruction: Create a functional component named ObservabilityDashboard that returns null for now.
steps.hint: Define a component with the exact name ObservabilityDashboard. You can use either a function declaration or arrow function syntax.
steps.seedCode:
import React, { useState } from 'react';

// Create the ObservabilityDashboard component here
steps.expectedOutcome: A functional component named ObservabilityDashboard is defined, returning null.
successCriteria: The ObservabilityDashboard component is defined and returns null.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've created the main ObservabilityDashboard component structure.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you've defined a component named ObservabilityDashboard that returns null.
steps.feedbackWrong: The component wasn't created correctly. Check that you've defined ObservabilityDashboard and it returns null.

steps.title: Initialize state for logs data
steps.instruction: Inside your ObservabilityDashboard component, use useState to initialize a state variable called 'logs' with an empty array as its initial value.
steps.hint: Call useState with [] to set up an empty array for storing log entries.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: initializing state for data
const [data, setData] = useState([]);
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will have a state variable 'logs' ready to store log entries for observability monitoring.
successCriteria: State variable 'logs' is declared using useState
Initial value is an empty array []
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've initialized the logs state correctly. This empty array will hold log entries for observability monitoring.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're using useState to declare a 'logs' state variable with an empty array as the initial value.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's try again. Use useState to create a state variable called 'logs' initialized to an empty array.

steps.title: Initialize state for metrics data
steps.instruction: Inside your ObservabilityDashboard component, use the useState hook to create a state variable called 'metrics' initialized as an empty object.
steps.hint: Add another useState call after your existing logs state. Remember to destructure the array: const [metrics, setMetrics] = useState({});
steps.analogousExample:
// Similar: initializing state for user data
const [userData, setUserData] = useState({});
steps.expectedOutcome: Your component will have two state variables: one for logs data and one for metrics data, both initialized as empty objects.
successCriteria: The metrics state is declared using useState and initialized as an empty object.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully initialized state for metrics data. This gives you a place to store metrics information like response times, error rates, and throughput.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure you're using useState to declare a state variable called 'metrics' and initialize it with an empty object {}.
steps.feedbackWrong: The metrics state isn't properly initialized. Remember to use useState to create a state variable called 'metrics' with an initial value of an empty object.

steps.title: Initialize state for traces data
steps.instruction: Inside your ObservabilityDashboard component, use the useState hook to initialize a state variable called 'traces' with an empty array as its initial value.
steps.hint: Add a new useState call similar to how you initialized logs and metrics state. The state variable should be named 'traces' and initialized with an empty array [].
steps.analogousExample:
// Similar: initializing state for an array
const [items, setItems] = useState([]);
steps.expectedOutcome: Your component will now have state variables ready to store logs, metrics, and traces data - the three pillars of observability.
successCriteria: A 'traces' state variable is initialized using useState with an empty array as the initial value.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully initialized state for traces data. Now you have all three observability pillars (logs, metrics, and traces) ready to store data.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're using useState to create a state variable named 'traces' initialized with an empty array [].
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's try again. You need to add a useState call inside your component to create a 'traces' state variable initialized with an empty array.

steps.title: Define handler to simulate log generation
steps.instruction: Inside the ObservabilityDashboard component, create a function named generateLog that adds a new sample log entry to the logs state.
steps.hint: Define a function that uses the setLogs updater to add a new log object to the existing logs array.
steps.expectedOutcome: A generateLog function is defined that will add new log entries to the logs state when called.
successCriteria: The generateLog function is defined inside the component and uses setLogs to add a new log object to the logs array.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've created a function that simulates log generation. This is essential for observability dashboards to demonstrate real-time log updates.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your generateLog function properly updates the logs state using setLogs with the previous logs array.
steps.feedbackWrong: The generateLog function isn't defined correctly. Remember to create a function that adds a new log object to the logs state array.

steps.title: Define handler to update metrics
steps.instruction: Inside your ObservabilityDashboard component, create a function named updateMetrics that updates the metrics state with sample values.
steps.hint: Define a function that calls setMetrics with an object containing sample metric data.
steps.expectedOutcome: A function named updateMetrics is defined that updates the metrics state with sample values.
successCriteria: The updateMetrics function is defined and calls setMetrics with an object containing sample metric data.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created the updateMetrics function to handle metrics updates.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've defined a function, but make sure it's named updateMetrics and calls setMetrics with an object.
steps.feedbackWrong: The updateMetrics function is not defined correctly. Create a function that updates the metrics state.

steps.title: Define handler to add trace data
steps.instruction: Create a function named addTrace that adds a new trace object to the traces state array. The function should accept a trace object as a parameter and update the state using the setTraces function.
steps.hint: Define a function that takes a trace parameter and uses setTraces with the previous state to add the new trace to the array.
steps.expectedOutcome: You should have a function named addTrace that updates the traces state by adding a new trace object to the array.
successCriteria: The addTrace function is defined, accepts a trace parameter, and uses setTraces to update the state array.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created the addTrace handler. This function will allow you to simulate adding trace data to your observability dashboard.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your addTrace function properly accepts a trace parameter and updates the traces state using setTraces.
steps.feedbackWrong: The addTrace function isn't defined correctly. Remember to create a function that takes a trace parameter and updates the traces state array.

steps.title: Create the main dashboard structure with three sections
steps.instruction: Return a div element from your ObservabilityDashboard component that contains three section elements for logs, metrics, and traces.
steps.hint: The return statement should output a div with three section elements inside it. Each section will later hold content for one observability pillar.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component now returns a div with three empty section elements, creating the basic layout structure for the observability dashboard.
successCriteria: The ObservabilityDashboard component returns a div containing exactly three section elements.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've created the main dashboard structure with three sections ready for logs, metrics, and traces content.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're returning a div with three section elements inside it.
steps.feedbackWrong: Check that you're returning a div element containing three section elements from your component.

steps.title: Add buttons and wire them to their respective handlers
steps.instruction: Add three buttons inside the first section: one labeled 'Generate Log' that calls generateLog on click, one labeled 'Update Metrics' that calls updateMetrics, and one labeled 'Add Trace' that calls addTrace.
steps.hint: Place the buttons inside the first <section> element. Use the onClick attribute to call each handler function.
steps.expectedOutcome: The first section will contain three interactive buttons that, when clicked, will trigger their respective observability data handlers.
successCriteria: Three buttons are present inside the first section with correct labels and onClick handlers wired to generateLog, updateMetrics, and addTrace.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added interactive buttons to generate observability data.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added some buttons, but check that all three are present with correct labels and onClick handlers.
steps.feedbackWrong: The buttons are missing or not correctly wired. Ensure you have three buttons with labels 'Generate Log', 'Update Metrics', 'Add Trace' and onClick handlers calling the respective functions.
